subject_line: The shape of "Occupy the Specter" in Subterranean
email_body:
Dear Richard,

Reading about Subterranean, I was struck by how its elegy for a father refuses to stay private: the poems sit somewhere between prose and centered lines, and they keep pulling in the decay that rides along with economic growth. "Occupy the Specter," the one conventional prose poem, seems to stand apart from the rest. I'd like to ask how you arrived at that in-between form, and why that single poem needed the plain block of prose.

subject_line: From Paddy on the Hardwood to a Fulbright in Ireland
email_body:
Dear Rus,

Paddy on the Hardwood followed basketball into Ireland years ago, and the Fulbright announced by NMSU sends you back there to look at race, immigration and sport. It's unusual for a writer to return to the same country with a different set of questions. I'd like to ask what has changed in the Irish game, and in your own way of seeing it, between the coach who wrote that book and the researcher going back now.

subject_line: Between A Mother Is an Intellectual Thing and Bewilder Meant
email_body:
Dear Kimberly,

Your UNT page describes A Mother Is an Intellectual Thing and the forthcoming Bewilder Meant as genre-defying, which is a striking turn for a poet whose The Opposite of Light won the Lexi Rudnitsky First Book Prize. Even the new title splits a familiar word in two. I'd like to ask what the essay form lets you think through about motherhood that the lyric poems in Systems for the Future of Feeling could not, and where Bewilder Meant sits between them.

subject_line: Two folklores in Lore: Mammoth Cave and the Ozarks
email_body:
Dear Davis,

Lore sets the folk traditions of the Mammoth Cave country you grew up in beside those of the Ozarks you adopted, and Ultima Thule drew partly on your own years as a park ranger underground. That decade as a guide seems to run under the later work too. I'd like to ask how an inherited folklore and an adopted one sit together on the page, and whether the Arkansas material arrived as a listener's or as a native's.

subject_line: From Fugue's End to the hills of Deep River Blues
email_body:
Dear Tony,

After four poetry collections, from Fugue's End to Greatest Hits, you turned to a regional crime thriller: Deep River Blues, set in the mountains of Eastern Tennessee. Poets who move into crime fiction often say the plot taught them something about the line, or the reverse. I'd like to ask what a crime novel's momentum demanded that your poems never had to, and why that Appalachian ground was the place for your first book-length story.

subject_line: Persephone in Enugu: The Middle Daughter
email_body:
Dear Chika,

The Middle Daughter carries the Hades and Persephone myth into Enugu, and it was a 2025 Townsend Prize finalist. A Greek abduction story is a bold frame for a Nigerian family novel, since the myth already decides how much of the year a daughter can be returned. I'd like to ask when the myth entered the book, at the start or partway through, and how far you let it steer the story of the daughter at its centre.

Claudia Rankine, choosing Love and the Eye for the Kore Press First Book Award, wrote that one leans into it because of all the ways it does not settle down. I'd like to ask what has refused to settle in the newer poems, and how editing has changed what you keep.

email_body:
Dear Edgar,

The linked untitled poems in Fixer, about the brothers clearing out your father's apartment, keep returning to a man who could repair almost anything except himself. I'd like to ask why that sequence needed to go untitled, and how the temp-job poems elsewhere in the book talk back to his kind of work.

subject_line: Heraclitus and the flotsam of The River Twice
email_body:
Dear Kathleen,

The River Twice takes its title from Heraclitus, yet the poems wander from letters to essay-like meditations, gathering what the Princeton description calls the remarkable and unremarkable flotsam of contemporary life. That mix of a philosopher's fragment and ordinary debris feels like the book's real method, and it won the UNT Rilke Prize. I'd like to ask how you decide when a small object earns its place beside the large questions, and whether the epistolary poems began as actual letters.

subject_line: The confrontation at the end of Blue-Skinned Gods
email_body:
Dear SJ,

In your TriQuarterly interview you described Blue-Skinned Gods as, at its core, a push and pull of power between a father and the boy he raises in an ashram to believe he is a child god, and said a confrontation became the only fitting ending. You also resisted calling it a coming-of-age story. I'd like to ask what you would call it instead, and how that father-son struggle compares with the families that Lucky has to deceive in Marriage of a Thousand Lies.

subject_line: From the big bang to the near future in Us From Nothing
email_body:
Dear Geoff,

Us From Nothing attempts something few prose poems would dare: a single serial epic moving through the milestones of human history, from the big bang to the near future. It appeared first with Wolsak & Wynn in Canada and then with Black Lawrence Press, a long way from the quieter rooms of Living Room. I'd like to ask how you chose which milestones made it in, and how the prose poem, usually a compact form, held up across that much time.

subject_line: Camp Levi and the horror film in How to Survive a Summer
email_body:
Dear Nick,

In How to Survive a Summer, Will Dillard is forced back to his teenage summer at Camp Levi not by a letter or a funeral but by a horror movie made about the camp. Garth Greenwell called the book an exuberantly queer Southern Gothic, and Rolling Stone noted the compassion you extend to the place itself. I'd like to ask why a horror film became the device that reopens Will's past, and how a Mississippi native finds compassion for a setting like that.

Dear Michelle,

If You Say So, your tenth book and fourth essay collection, arrives while you also answer readers' questions each week in Slate's Care and Feeding column. Before it came the 2022 novel that, as your department newsletter reports, took inspiration from a former student. Few writers move between advice, essay and fiction so steadily. I'd like to ask how giving advice in public has changed the voice of your essays, and what you learned from building a novel around someone you once taught.
